Among the hierarchy of the various interstellar structures that exist, the formation of clumps, i.e. the parsec-scale progenitors of star clusters, has been identified as a pivotal stage of the star formation process. The study of molecular gas propertes on clump to cloud scale indeed showed that clumps are dynamically decoupled from the rest of their parent molecular clouds. Understanding the origin of this decoupling, along with its impact on the determination of the core and stellar mass functions, must therefore be at the centre of any research that attempts to solve the star cluster formation puzzle. Here we popose to map the density structure and velocity field of 259 clumps, all located at a distance of 2.5 to 5kpc, for which uniform datasets on both larger-scale (parent molecular clouds) and smaller-scale (cores) exist. The proposed ALMA observations will threfore provide, for the first time, a consistent and detailed picture of gas flows towards the formation of star clusters, from tens of parsecs down to ~1000 AU scale. This is the Panta Rei large program.

proposal_abstract: Magnetic fields are acknowledged for their dynamic role in the interstellar medium (ISM), especially in star forming regions, as shown by the Planck mission. However, measuring the magnetic field strength accurately is complex and demands high sensitivity and precision due to the challenges posed by the Zeeman effect. Our proposed ZeeSMoS study aims to identify the most intense compact emission spots from molecules sensitive to the Zeeman effect, such as CN and SO. We plan to map CN and SO emissions, along with continuum emission, across the closest 538 sources that have been previously mapped by ALMAGAL survey. Utilizing various structure finding algorithms, we will compile a catalog of compact and intense CN, SO, and continuum sources suitable for future Zeeman effect observations with ALMA. This catalog will facilitate investigations into the scaling relationship between magnetic field strength and density, specifically to address whether the power law index follows a n^1/2 or n^0.65 power law. Additionally, by focusing on regions previously mapped by ALMA in full polarization, we open possibilities for future estimates of total magnetic field strengths.

proposal_abstract: What happens to molecular gas when galaxies shut down? Do galaxies stop forming stars because they run out of gas or because their molecular clouds become passive and unable to collapse? What is the origin of molecular gas in retired galaxies? To answer these questions we propose to survey of 54 galaxies in CO 2-1 chosen to be 0.5 dex below the main sequence, over a relatively narrow range of masses and a wide range of integrated star formation rates. The galaxies are selected from the AMUSING++ survey, so they have a full complement of integral field unit information about their stellar and ionized gas components. We will dramatically improve in sensitivity over previous targeted surveys of early type galaxies with IFU data. With these observations we will: 1) establish the importance of gas consumption and gas stabilization in galaxy quenching, 2) determine the local scaling relations between star formation, gas, and stellar mass, and 3) characterize the kinematics of the gas in comparison to the stars and offer clues to the origin of the gas in these systems.

proposal_abstract: Galaxy mergers are predicted to radically transform their constituents, eventually causing them to transition into red and dead passive galaxies. Observations have confirmed an excess of recent and rapidly quenched galaxies amongst post-mergers. However, a conundrum remains, because post-mergers have also been found to contain an excess of molecular gas. How is it that galaxies quench with such ample gas reservoirs? One possible answer is timescales, because the quenching signature is linked to spectral features that are sensitive to timescales of 500-800 Myr whereas the samples for which gas fractions have been measured (and found to be abundant) are likely to represent mergers that have only recently coalesced. Hence, a potential solution is one in which recent post-mergers still contain ample gas, but that over the course of 0.5-1 Gyr this gas is depleted and star formation shuts down. We propose to test this scenario by measuring the gas fraction as a function of time since post-merger in 52 galaxies, a timescale that we can measure based on neural network predictions. This will be the first observational study of the evolution of galaxies as a function of time since merger.

proposal_abstract: Powerful outflow is considered as an important mechanism to quench star formation in massive galaxy. A luminous AGN is supposed to drive an outflow to high velocity (e.g., over 1000 km/s). Recently a sample of ULIRGs with extremely fast outflows (1000--2000 km/s) was reported. However, these ULIRGs only show AGN signatures in large scale, i.e., fast outflow and ionization cone, while the mid-IR radiation from pc-scale dusty torus is not detected. The combination of large scale AGN activity and non-detection of AGN in the central region suggests "fading AGNs" in the ULIRGs, and the observed extreme outflow could be relics of AGN activity in a past active episode, i.e., "fossil outflows". In order to determine whether the molecular gas clouds where stars form have been affected by the AGN fossil outflows, we propose observations of CO(3-2) to trace the kinematics of molecular gas and determine the feedback effect of molecular outflow on the host. This study opens a window to understand the cumulative feedback effect of AGN on its host galaxy in a full AGN cycle.

proposal_abstract: How complex organic molecules (COMs) formed in star-forming regions is still an open question. The deuterium-to-hydrogen (D/H) ratio is frequently used to trace the physical conditions in the formation history of interstellar species. Methanol (CH3OH), the most abundant COM, has been found to have overabundant deuterated isotopologues in low-mass protostars, espeically the multiply deuterated ones. This is considered as an indicator of molecules forming in cold environments, likely during the pre-stellar phase. On the other hand, studies of higher-mass protostars revealed decreasing CH2DOH/CH3OH ratios with mass, whereas the CHD2OH/CH2DOH ratios are on the same level between low- and high-mass sources. The former suggests a warmer pre-stellar phase in high-mass protostars, but the latter introduces a quesition of whether successive deuteration has the same mechanism as single deuteration. If not, it may affect our current application of deuterium chemistry. Unfortunately, there lacks of high quality data for high-mass sources to study the successive deuteration of COMs. Therefore, we propose to target the five most abundant (multiply) deuterated COMs in ~20 high-mass hot cores.

proposal_abstract: Star formation is a multi-scale process that spans many orders of magnitude in spatial scales and gas densities. Among the hierarchy of the various interstellar structures that exist, the formation of clumps, i.e. the parsec-scale progenitors of star clusters, has been identified as a pivotal stage of the star formation process. The study of molecular gas propertes on clump to cloud scale indeed showed that clumps are dynamically decoupled from the rest of their parent molecular clouds. Understanding the origin of this decoupling, along with its impact on the determination of the core and stellar mass functions, must therefore be at the centre of any research that attempts to solve the star cluster formation puzzle. Here we popose to map the density structure and velocity field of 259 clumps, all located at a distance of 2.5 to 5kpc, for which uniform datasets on both larger-scale (parent molecular clouds) and smaller-scale (cores) exist. The proposed ALMA observations will threfore provide, for the first time, a consistent and detailed picture of gas flows towards the formation of star clusters, from tens of parsecs down to ~1000 AU scale. This is the Panta Rei large program.

Spectroscopic follow-up cuts through this 2D degeneracy, but less than ten fields have their submm-detected sources confirmed spectroscopically. Using efficient snapshot-style observations centred on the [CII] line, we will test the protocluster membership of 44 fields containing a total of 555 sources. Robust detections of their [CII] and continuum emission will allow us to directly answer fundamental questions, including, what is the contribution of overdense regions to stellar build-up in the z = 4 - 7 Universe? Do the gas and star-formation rate densities evolve in the z > 4 Universe? And have we already observed LambdaCDM breaking protoclusters in 2D maps?

proposal_abstract: Radio-loud AGNs drive galaxy evolution through kinetic feedback, yet their millimeter (mm) properties remain largely unexplored. While the northern 3CR catalog has defined AGN physics for decades, its southern equivalent, the G4Jy-3CRE catalog (S @178 MHz > 9 Jy, Dec < -5°), provides the fundamental sample for the SKA era. This proposal is based on ACA Band 3 observations of a selected sample of G4Jy-3CRE sources. This survey will: (i) obtain sub-mm and mm observations to pave the path towards ALMA data at higher angular resolution; (ii) explore connection between nuclear emission observed at sub-mm and mm frequencies with those, already available, at radio, mid-IR, optical and X-ray energies; (iii) anchor broadband SEDs to quantify the core energetic output; (iv) execute a simultaneous search for CO(1-0) emission in about 20% of the sample to probe molecular gas. These ACA observations are strictly mandatory to characterize the core flux, establishing the spectral constraints required for future high-resolution 12-m array follow-ups. This project will have a crucial legacy value on exploring SKA-ALMA synergies for the most powerful radio sources.

proposal_abstract: What are the optical and near-infrared counterparts to sub-millimeter galaxies (SMGs)? Historically, the answer to this question has been limited to the brightest of sub-mm sources imposing strong bias on our understanding of this population. Now, JWST is sensitive enough to detect the optical/near-IR counterparts to SMGs over a broad luminosity range; however, associating SMGs with their counterparts at shorter wavelengths is complicated by the large beam sizes of ground-based sub-mm facilities (~11"). To overcome this problem, we propose an ALMA Band 7 survey targeting every SMG in the COSMOS-Web JWST survey area (0.54 deg2) that does not already have an observation in the ALMA archive. We will use ALMA to localize sub-mm emission relative to COSMOS-Web (JWST imaging) and COSMOS-3D (NIRCam/F444W wide-field slitless spectroscopy) to study the stellar properties, redshifts, and morphologies for a flux-limited S_850 > 2 mJy sample. This program will complete a legacy data product for a representative sample of 696 SMGs in just 4.9 total hours of ALMA/Band 7 time.

Historically, the answer to this question has been limited to the brightest of sub-mm sources imposing strong bias on our understanding of this population. Now, JWST is sensitive enough to detect the optical/near-IR counterparts to SMGs over a broad luminosity range; however, associating SMGs with their counterparts at shorter wavelengths is complicated by the large beam sizes of ground-based sub-mm facilities (~11"). To overcome this problem, we propose an ALMA Band 7 survey targeting every SMG in the COSMOS-Web JWST survey area (0.54 deg2) that does not already have an observation in the ALMA archive. We will use ALMA to localize sub-mm emission relative to COSMOS-Web (JWST imaging) and COSMOS-3D (NIRCam/F444W wide-field slitless spectroscopy) to study the stellar properties, redshifts, and morphologies for a flux-limited S_850 > 2 mJy sample. This program will complete a legacy data product for a representative sample of 696 SMGs in just 4.9 total hours of ALMA/Band 7 time.

proposal_abstract: We request multi-transition CO observations to measure accurate gas masses for a golden sample of 16 galaxies at z=4-5. These objects are representative of massive (M_star = 10^10-10^11 Msun), star-forming (SFR = 100-1000 Msun/yr), primeval galaxies. All of them have (1) ALMA [CII] data at sub-kpc resolutions providing the rotation curve and cold gas distribution, (2) JWST images providing the stellar mass distribution, and (3) VLA CO(1-0) data providing a first-order estimate of the gas mass. To break the disk-halo degeneracy between the gas contribution and the dark matter (DM) contribution, we need to estimate accurate gas masses, so the alpha_CO factor, for each individual galaxy. We will (1) construct CO SLEDs to measure alpha_CO and the gas mass, (2) fit rotation curves accounting for the contributions of gas, stars, and DM, (3) study the evolution of scaling laws (Tully-Fisher relation and more), (4) study star-formation laws using gas and star-formation-rate maps. Our project will exploit a unique ALMA+VLA+JWST synergy to measure the total mass content (gas, stars, and DM) of massive galaxies at z=4-5, tracing DM in a cosmic epoch that has been out of reach until now.

proposal_abstract: Of the dozens of mid-infrared spectra of protoplanetary disks taken to-date, one source stands out: the very low-mass star 2MASS J16053215-1933159 (J1605). Broad features detected in Spitzer spectra had no known origin, and the lack of the typical 10 micron dust feature was puzzling. JWST-MIRI data finally shed light on this source: an extremely carbon-rich disk, with many molecular species detected, including the first C6H6 disk detection. The high C/O of the inner disk may be related to the efficient radial drift of dust grains that occurs in disks around low-mass stars. However, ALMA data are needed to provide the whole picture, in particular by allowing us to measure the dust mass to determine how little mm-sized dust is left at this age and by characterizing the outer disk gas, especially the C/O ratio. We propose a deep integration of J1605 to detect: 1) the continuum to measure the dust mass, 2) 13CO and C18O to measure the gas mass, 3) C2H to determine the C/O ratio in the outer disk to compare with the inner disk, and 4) potentially serendipitously detect additional lines to help understand this extraordinary disk, which is a precursor to planetary systems like TRAPPIST-1.

proposal_abstract: It is evident that we need to probe larger samples of protoplanetary disks so that another 7 years do not have to pass before the next PDS 70– or WISPIT 2–like system is discovered. In the spirit of a community effort, we propose to use the ACA to survey young stellar objects (YSOs) in the LST range that is currently heavily undersubscribed (RA = 20h–1h), following the Call for Proposals. We have identified these objects based on previous YSO catalogues and a requirement for a minimum level of IR excess. The goal is to systematically obtain mm-fluxes and 12CO line observations of new protoplanetary disks while maximising the use of ALMA. One of these disks could be the next system clearly hosting forming planets that will drive the next major advances in the planet formation field. Any newly discovered bright disk can then be followed up with the 12 m array or other facilities. To maximise the scientific return for the community, we are happy to lift the proprietary time on the data so that the community can use the results as they become available.

Our understanding of SMBHB evolution, their gravitational wave (GW) emission, the interpretation of current SMBHB GW observatory findings, and predictions for future SMBHB GW observatories, are all limited by this paucity of confirmed SMBHB. We show that the unprecedented resolution of the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT), its relatively high radio frequency, its increasing sensitivity, among other factors, combine to make it a powerful (but as yet unproven) hunter of SMBHB down to sub-pc (and even milli-pc) separations, thus strong GW regimes. We propose an economical and efficient ACA program to complete 230 GHz flux measurements of all ALMA accessible SMBHB candidates with estimated separations of <=100 pc and without existing such flux measurements. A fully 230 GHz characterized SMBHB sample we will enable an optimal selection of targets for which the highest resolution ALMA and EHT observations and monitoring can attempt to confirm new SMBHB candidates, and track - through resolved imaging - the orbits of these in their GW emitting phase.

proposal_abstract: How complex organic molecules (COMs) formed in star-forming regions is still an open question. The deuterium-to-hydrogen (D/H) ratio is frequently used to trace the physical conditions in the formation history of interstellar species. Methanol (CH3OH), the most abundant COM, has been found to have overabundant deuterated isotopologues in low-mass protostars, espeically the multiply deuterated ones. This is considered as an indicator of molecules forming in cold environments, likely during the pre-stellar phase. On the other hand, studies of higher-mass protostars revealed decreasing CH2DOH/CH3OH ratios with mass, whereas the CHD2OH/CH2DOH ratios are on the same level between low- and high-mass sources. The former suggests a warmer pre-stellar phase in high-mass protostars, but the latter introduces a quesition of whether successive deuteration has the same mechanism as single deuteration. If not, it may affect our current application of deuterium chemistry. Unfortunately, there lacks of high quality data for high-mass sources to study the successive deuteration of COMs. Therefore, we propose to target the five most abundant (multiply) deuterated COMs in ~20 high-mass hot cores.

proposal_abstract: Star formation is a multi-scale process that spans many orders of magnitude in spatial scales and gas densities. Among the hierarchy of the various interstellar structures that exist, the formation of clumps, i.e. the parsec-scale progenitors of star clusters, has been identified as a pivotal stage of the star formation process. The study of molecular gas propertes on clump to cloud scale indeed showed that clumps are dynamically decoupled from the rest of their parent molecular clouds. Understanding the origin of this decoupling, along with its impact on the determination of the core and stellar mass functions, must therefore be at the centre of any research that attempts to solve the star cluster formation puzzle. Here we popose to map the density structure and velocity field of 259 clumps, all located at a distance of 2.5 to 5kpc, for which uniform datasets on both larger-scale (parent molecular clouds) and smaller-scale (cores) exist. The proposed ALMA observations will threfore provide, for the first time, a consistent and detailed picture of gas flows towards the formation of star clusters, from tens of parsecs down to ~1000 AU scale. This is the Panta Rei large program.

proposal_abstract: The importance of massive stars is recognized 100 years ago, but their formation remains unclear due to their large distance, high extinction, and short lifetime. Massive clumps as the habitat of massive stars fragment into dense cores, where protostars are actively forming. However, our understanding of them is shrouded by their (sub-)millimeter thickness. Recent ALMA 1.3 mm large surveys have found that individual dense cores are generally becoming optically thick when resolution is as high as thousand-au, so their masses should be more or less underetimated, which can't be fixed by single band observation. By combining proposed and archived datasets, we are about to give accurate estimations of core masses in >100 massive clumps. We will be standing at the best dual-band point of answering the following questions. 1) How much gas is locked in cores? 2) How does core mass vary with time? 3) And how does core mass function (CMF) look like and how is it mapped to stellar initial mass function (IMF)?

proposal_abstract: Recent redshift searches of DSFGs are enabling full spectroscopic follow up; however, exploiting this with ALMA is challenging, as the large overheads favour deep studies of individual sources. The ANGELS project circumvents this problem by targeting continuum bands while including as many lines as possible. This project has successfully mapped Bands 3 through 8 on 90 sources. Here, we ask for 12 hrs of Band 9 and 14.2 hrs of Band 10 observations to provide the most detailed view on the dust continuum in a targeted survey of 71 of the well-studied sources. These data will improve Herschel astrometry by two orders of magnitude and provide pixel-to-pixel maps of the dust temperature inside these DSFGs. proposal_abstract: Star formation is a multi-scale process that spans many orders of magnitude in spatial scales and gas densities. Among the hierarchy of the various interstellar structures that exist, the formation of clumps, i.e. the parsec-scale progenitors of star clusters, has been identified as a pivotal stage of the star formation process. The study of molecular gas propertes on clump to cloud scale indeed showed that clumps are dynamically decoupled from the rest of their parent molecular clouds. Understanding the origin of this decoupling, along with its impact on the determination of the core and stellar mass functions, must therefore be at the centre of any research that attempts to solve the star cluster formation puzzle. Here we popose to map the density structure and velocity field of 259 clumps, all located at a distance of 2.5 to 5kpc, for which uniform datasets on both larger-scale (parent molecular clouds) and smaller-scale (cores) exist. The proposed ALMA observations will threfore provide, for the first time, a consistent and detailed picture of gas flows towards the formation of star clusters, from tens of parsecs down to ~1000 AU scale. This is the Panta Rei large program.

proposal_abstract: The life cycle and evolution of a galaxy is closely tied to the transformation of gas into stars. Empirical scaling relations between the stellar mass, star formation rate, and molecular gas, typically traced by CO, show considerable diversity from galaxy-to-galaxy. In order to understand these observed variations, we need to assess the mass of dense molecular gas directly responsible for star formation, which is typically traced by HCN emission. HCN observations in the literature are primarily biased toward galaxies which lie above the star-forming main sequence (SFMS). Only a few galaxies that lie on or below the SFMS, in the so-called green valley, have been observed in dense gas. We propose HCN (1-0) observations for a sample of 25 galaxies that are in the green valley and have been previously observed in CO with ALMA. In addition, we propose to observe 18 galaxies on the SFMS to combine with existing data to complete a robust comparison sample. We will test if the offset of green valley galaxies from the SFMS is a result of low dense gas star formation efficiency or dense gas fraction. We aim to answer the question: Is dense gas star formation efficiency truly a constant?

In order to understand these observed variations, we need to assess the mass of dense molecular gas directly responsible for star formation, which is typically traced by HCN emission. HCN observations in the literature are primarily biased toward galaxies which lie above the star-forming main sequence (SFMS). Only a few galaxies that lie on or below the SFMS, in the so-called green valley, have been observed in dense gas. We propose HCN (1-0) observations for a sample of 25 galaxies that are in the green valley and have been previously observed in CO with ALMA. In addition, we propose to observe 18 galaxies on the SFMS to combine with existing data to complete a robust comparison sample. We will test if the offset of green valley galaxies from the SFMS is a result of low dense gas star formation efficiency or dense gas fraction. We aim to answer the question: Is dense gas star formation efficiency truly a constant?

proposal_abstract: Star formation is a multi-scale process that spans many orders of magnitude in spatial scales and gas densities. Among the hierarchy of the various interstellar structures that exist, the formation of clumps, i.e. the parsec-scale progenitors of star clusters, has been identified as a pivotal stage of the star formation process. The study of molecular gas propertes on clump to cloud scale indeed showed that clumps are dynamically decoupled from the rest of their parent molecular clouds. Understanding the origin of this decoupling, along with its impact on the determination of the core and stellar mass functions, must therefore be at the centre of any research that attempts to solve the star cluster formation puzzle. Here we popose to map the density structure and velocity field of 259 clumps, all located at a distance of 2.5 to 5kpc, for which uniform datasets on both larger-scale (parent molecular clouds) and smaller-scale (cores) exist. The proposed ALMA observations will threfore provide, for the first time, a consistent and detailed picture of gas flows towards the formation of star clusters, from tens of parsecs down to ~1000 AU scale. This is the Panta Rei large program.

proposal_abstract: A major impediment to star formation (SF) law studies at z>4 is the systematic uncertainty in converting [CII] luminosities into molecular gas masses. To mitigate this, we request [CI] 2-1 and 1-0 observations towards 16 massive galaxies at z=4-5, for which JWST photometry and ALMA [CII] are already available. By jointly analyzing [CI], [CII] with CO and multi-frequency dust continuum (available in the requested tunings and/or ALMA archive), our objectives are to: (1) infer the excitation temperatures and gas masses; (2) measure the carbon neutral fraction; (3) validate gas mass conversions and examine the level of subthermal excitation. The proposed observations will be the first of such kind at z~4, for which both [CI] lines and [CII] are available, providing direct constraints on the cold ISM conditions. We will explore how gas excitation/ionization states and supply may be affected by AGN and/or interactions at z~4. We will test the validity of common assumptions (e.g. LTE, dust-gas coupling) in star-forming galaxies at z>4, and progress toward more accurate gas mass conversions, crucial for advancing SF law studies at z>4.
